terms.definition: The Domain Name System: a distributed directory that translates names like example.com into IP addresses. Answers are cached at many levels.
The numeric address a machine uses on the internet, like 93.184.216.34 (IPv4) or a longer IPv6 address.
Transmission Control Protocol: delivers a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two machines, resending anything that gets lost.
User Datagram Protocol: sends individual packets with no delivery or ordering guarantees, which makes it simple and fast.
Transport Layer Security: encrypts a connection and proves the server’s identity. It is the “S” in HTTPS.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request–response protocol browsers and APIs use. A client sends a method and path; the server answers with a status code and a body.
A version of HTTP that sends many requests at once over a single connection (multiplexing) and compresses headers.
HTTP over QUIC, a transport built on UDP. A lost packet only delays its own stream instead of every request on the connection.
When one slow or lost item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it.
The time for a message to go from one machine to another and for the reply to come back.
Reusing an open connection for several requests, which avoids paying for a new TCP and TLS handshake each time.
Application Programming Interface: the contract one program offers others, listing the operations they can call and the data they exchange.
A style of HTTP API built around resources (nouns) identified by URLs and manipulated with standard methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.
A remote procedure call framework that sends compact binary messages (Protocol Buffers) over HTTP/2 and supports streaming.
A language-neutral way to define messages in a schema and encode them as compact binary.
A long-lived, two-way connection between browser and server, so either side can send messages at any time.
A one-way stream of messages from server to browser over a normal HTTP response.
The client makes a request that the server holds open until there is news, then the client immediately asks again.
Returning a large list in pages. Cursor-based pagination stays correct when items are added during browsing.
Changing an API without breaking existing clients, for example by adding fields instead of renaming them or by publishing /v2 alongside /v1.
A running program with its own memory space. Processes are isolated from each other by the operating system.
A unit of execution inside a process. Threads share the process’s memory, which makes them cheap to start but easy to get wrong.
When the CPU stops running one thread and starts another, saving and restoring their state. Frequent switching wastes time.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads, for example two threads both reading a counter as 5 and both writing 6.
A way to let only one thread at a time run a piece of code or touch a piece of data.
Two or more threads each waiting for a lock the other holds, so none of them can continue.
A single thread that waits for I/O events and runs a short handler for each. It serves many connections without a thread per connection.
Starting a read or write and doing other work until it finishes, instead of blocking a thread while waiting.
A fixed set of reusable threads that pick up tasks from a queue, which caps how much work runs at once.
A database that stores data in tables of rows and columns, links tables by keys and is queried with SQL.
An umbrella term for non-relational databases (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) that trade some features for scale or flexibility.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees a database transaction gives you.
A group of reads and writes that succeeds or fails as one unit.
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other’s unfinished work, from read committed to serializable.
An anomaly where two transactions each read the same data, make decisions based on it and write different rows, breaking a rule neither broke alone.
A database that stores values under keys and looks them up by key, which is simple and very fast.
A database that stores self-contained documents (often JSON) and can query fields inside them.
A database that groups data by row key into flexible column families, built for very large write-heavy workloads.
A database that stores nodes and the relationships between them and is fast at traversing those relationships.
Organizing tables so each fact is stored once, which avoids inconsistent copies.
Deliberately storing copies of data to make reads faster, at the cost of keeping the copies in sync.
An extra data structure that lets a database find rows without scanning the whole table, at the cost of storage and slower writes.
A balanced tree of sorted keys with many children per node, so any key is a few disk reads away. The default index in most relational databases.
Log-structured merge tree: buffers writes in memory, flushes them as sorted files and merges files in the background. Fast writes, more work for reads.
An index on several columns in a fixed order. It helps queries that filter on a leading prefix of those columns.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index alone.
When one logical write causes several physical writes, for example updating indexes or rewriting files during compaction.
Reading every row of a table to answer a query, which is what happens without a useful index.
The time between sending a request and receiving its response.
How much work a system completes per unit of time, such as requests per second.
How much data a link can carry per second.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall. p99 latency of 200 ms means 99% of requests finish within 200 ms.
The latency of the slowest requests, such as p99 or p99.9. At scale, most users hit the tail somewhere.
The total time a request may take, split across the steps it passes through.
Sending a second copy of a slow request to another replica and using whichever answers first, to cut tail latency.
Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine. Simple, but limited and with a single point of failure.
Handling more load by adding more machines and spreading work across them.
A service that keeps no per-user data between requests, so any instance can handle any request.
A component that spreads incoming requests across several servers and stops sending to unhealthy ones.
Balancing by connection (IP and port) without looking inside requests. Fast, but unaware of URLs or headers.
Balancing by request content such as path, header or cookie, which enables smarter routing at more cost.
Sending each new request to the next server in turn.
Sending each new request to the server with the fewest requests in progress.
A periodic probe that tells a load balancer whether an instance is able to serve traffic.
Picking two servers at random and sending the request to the less busy one. Spreads load almost as well as checking every server.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down.
Keeping a copy of frequently used data in faster storage so later reads skip the slow source.
The share of requests a cache answers itself. A hit rate of 90% means only 10% of requests reach the source.
The application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and stores the result in the cache.
A cache that loads missing data from the source itself, so the application only ever talks to the cache.
Every write goes to the cache and the source at the same time, keeping them in sync at the cost of slower writes.
Writes go to the cache first and reach the source later, which is fast but risks losing data if the cache fails.
Time to live: how long a cached value or DNS answer may be used before it must be refreshed.
Least recently used: when the cache is full, drop the item that has gone unused the longest.
Least frequently used: when the cache is full, drop the item that has been used the fewest times.
Removing or updating cached copies when the source data changes.
Many requests miss the cache at the same moment (often when a hot key expires) and all hit the database together.
Content delivery network: servers around the world that cache content close to users.
Keeping copies of the same data on several machines for availability, durability or read capacity.
One node (the leader or primary) accepts writes and streams them to followers (replicas) that serve reads.
Several nodes accept writes and exchange them, which needs a plan for conflicting writes.
Clients write to and read from several replicas directly and use quorums to decide what is current.
The delay before a write on the leader appears on a follower.
A guarantee that after you write something, your own later reads see it.
Promoting a replica to take over when the leader fails.
The minimum number of replicas that must take part in a read or write. With R + W > N, every read overlaps the latest write.
Splitting data across machines so each one holds only part of it.
Assigning keys to shards by key range, like A–F and G–M. Good for range scans, prone to hot spots.
Assigning keys to shards by a hash of the key, which spreads load evenly but loses ordering.
A shard or key that receives far more traffic than the rest.
Moving data between shards when you add or remove machines.
Placing keys and nodes on a ring so that adding or removing a node moves only the keys next to it.
Giving each physical node many points on a consistent-hashing ring so load spreads more evenly.
A buffer between producers and consumers. Each message is processed by one consumer.
Each published message is delivered to every subscriber of its topic.
A consumer’s signal that it has finished a message, so the queue can stop redelivering it.
Every message is delivered, but some may arrive more than once, so consumers must handle duplicates.
Messages are never duplicated, but some may be lost.
The effect of each message happens once. In practice this comes from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
Where messages go after failing too many times, so they stop blocking the queue and can be inspected.
Slowing down or rejecting producers when consumers cannot keep up, instead of letting work pile up without limit.
Every read sees the most recent completed write.
If writes stop, all replicas eventually return the same value; until then reads may be stale.
Operations that depend on each other are seen in the same order by everyone; unrelated ones may be seen in any order.
The system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data and every operation took effect at one instant.
A failure that splits machines into groups that cannot talk to each other.
During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency (refuse some requests) and availability (answer, possibly with stale data).
Extends CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.
Getting several machines to agree on one value or order of events, even when some fail.
A consensus algorithm with an elected leader that replicates a log of commands to followers.
Capping how many requests a client may make in a period of time.
A rate limiter where tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one; bursts are allowed up to the bucket size.
A rate limiter that queues requests and lets them out at a steady rate, smoothing bursts.
Counting requests per fixed interval, such as per minute. Simple, but allows double bursts at window edges.
Counting requests over the last N seconds at any moment, which avoids the edge bursts of fixed windows.
An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
A unique id sent with a request so the server can recognise a retry and return the first result instead of acting twice.
Retrying a failed request after waiting longer each time, so a struggling service gets room to recover.
Random variation added to retry delays so many clients do not retry at the same instant.
Quick, rounded arithmetic to size a system before designing it: requests per second, storage, bandwidth.
Queries (or requests) per second.
The number of distinct users who use a product on a given day.
How much busier the busiest period is than the average, often 2–5× for consumer products.
Average number of items in a system = arrival rate × average time each spends inside (L = λW).
